text: Nicholas Kipyator Kiprono arap Biwott (22 February 1940 – 11 July 2017) was a Kenyan businessman, politician, and philanthropist who served in the governments of Jomo Kenyatta and Daniel arap Moi, holding eight senior civil servant and ministerial positions, including Minister of State (1979–82), Minister of Energy (1984–1985, 1990), Minister of East African and Regional Co-operation (1998–99), and Minister of Regional Development, Science, and Technology (1982). He was widely regarded as one of the most powerful and competent ministers under President Moi and a key figure in advancing regional cooperation. Former president Uhuru Kenyatta praised Biwott as a "patriot and diligent leader, who spent decades building schools and hospitals and spearheading every other kind of development including marketing Kenya abroad." Born on 22 February 1940 in Tot, Chebior village, Elgeyo-Marakwet District, Rift Valley Province of British Kenya, to Maria Soti and Joseph Cheserem Soti, a market trader and cattle herder in Eldoret, Biwott attended Tambach Intermediate School (1951–1954) and later Kapsabet High School. After finishing secondary school in 1959, he began working at the Department of Information in Eldoret and published the Kalenjin monthly newsletter with Kendagor Bett. He studied at the University of Melbourne, Australia, from 1962 to 1964, earning a Bachelor of Arts in Economics and Political Science and a Diploma in Public Administration. He served as District Officer in Nkubu, South Imenti Division, Meru District (1964–1965), returned to Melbourne in 1966 for a master's degree in Economics under a Commonwealth scholarship, and completed it in 1968. Biwott entered government service in 1965 as District Officer in South Imenti and Tharaka, Meru District (January 1965–June 1966), where he implemented 'harambee' community fundraising for irrigation projects, roads, health centres, schools, employment at Igoji quarries, and coffee and tea planting. He also played a central role in the 'Land Transfer' programme under the 'Million Acres' scheme and helped rehabilitate the Mau Mau, persuading them to discontinue violence and resettling many on their own land. After his master's degree, he worked in the Ministry of Agriculture, GOK, as Personal Assistant to Minister Bruce MacKenzie (1968–1970), coordinating cereal production, marketing, fertiliser policy, and research into wheat and maize strains, and guiding Kenya’s regional policy with the East African Council of Ministers. In 1971, he moved to the Treasury as Senior Secretary under Minister of Finance and Economic Planning Mwai Kibaki, creating and heading the External Aid Division and technical assistance program, facilitating the establishment of the French School in Nairobi (now Lycee Denis Diderot), the French Cultural Centre with Alliance de Francais, and the German Friedrich Ebert Stiftung Foundation with Goethe Institut. In late 1978, he transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs on President Kenyatta’s personal recommendation to work with Vice-President Daniel arap Moi. In 1974, he ran unsuccessfully for Keiyo South Constituency; in 1979, he won the seat on the KANU ticket and retained it in 1983, 1988, 1992, 1997, and 2002, losing it in the 2007 election to Jackson Kiptanui Arap Kamai of the Orange Democratic Party (ODM), which won all but one of KANU’s Rift Valley seats. Following the 2002 election, he served on the Devolution Committee of the Constitution of Kenya Review Commission and abstained from the 2005 Constitutional Referendum, stating the draft constitution would divide the country along ethnic lines; it was rejected. In 2005, he contested the leadership of KANU but lost to Uhuru Kenyatta after a Kenyan High Court decision. Biwott served as Under Secretary (1974–1978) in the Ministry of Home Affairs under Moi, then as Deputy Permanent Secretary in the Office of the President (1978–1979) after Kenyatta’s death. After being elected MP in 1979, he returned to the Office of the President as Minister of State (1979–1982) responsible for science and technology, cabinet affairs, land settlement, and immigration, during which the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) was established. In September 1982, he became Minister of Regional Development, Science, and Technology, creating the Lake Basin Development Authority and the Kerio Valley Development Authority based on regional models from Australia and Tennessee. In September 1983, he was appointed Minister of Energy and Regional Development, and in March 1988, after ministry reorganisation, became Minister of Energy, holding the post until January 1991. During this period, he established the National Oil Corporation, built national oil storage facilities near Nairobi connected to the Mombasa refinery, extended the pipeline from Nairobi to Kisumu and Eldoret, and advanced rural electrification, the Sondu Miriu Dam, the Masinga Multi-Purpose Dam, the Kiambere Hydro Electric Dam, and the Turkwell Hydro Electric Multi-Purpose Dam. From 1991 until 1997, he held no government position, then returned as Minister of State in the Office of the President of East Africa in 1997, becoming Minister of East African and Regional Co-operation (1998–1999). He played a central role in COMESA, coordinating legislation for an East African Road Network and an East African Legislative Assembly, and serving as Chairman of both COMESA and the East Africa Council of Ministers. In September 1999, his portfolio expanded to include Trade and Industry, Tourism, and East African Cooperation (1999–2001), during which he established a Tourist Trust Fund with the European Union, set up the Tourist Police, and re-introduced the East Africa Safari Rallies. He was praised as "the hardest working minister of tourism Kenya has ever had" and "the best minister of tourism in 25 years." In May 2001, he continued as Minister of Trade and Industry and East African Tourism (2001–2002), establishing the Small Medium Trade Trust Fund with the European Union, introducing an Intellectual Property bill passed as an Act, achieving a free trade area with COMESA, establishing the Africa Trade Insurance Agency to cover foreign investments against political risk, and serving as Chairman of the African Caribbean Pacific Group (ACP) at the World Trade Organization. Biwott was a successful entrepreneur, having worked with his father in a fruit and vegetable business in Eldoret as a teenager, borrowing money to start a meat and egg sideline, and later forming ABC Foods in the late 1960s. In 1969, at age 29, he purchased the Eldoret Town International Harvester (IH) dealership (now FMD trading as Lima Ltd), a dairy farm, started an importer-exporter business in 1972, bought two wheat farms in 1974, established the sole agency for IH agricultural tractors and implements in 1975, and acquired a local air operator in 1977 (now Air Kenya). His business strategy of acquiring small or failing businesses and reinvesting in them proved successful, making him one of Kenya’s wealthiest businessmen. His businesses employ thousands and one of his major shareholder companies has been among Kenya’s top 10 corporate taxpayers. He supported education, health, and small business development, establishing the Mbegu Trust in 2008 to develop education and opportunity in Kenya. He actively promoted girls’ education by building schools such as the Maria Soti Educational Centre and Biwott Secondary School, and founded and patronized the Keiyo South Education Foundation, providing bursaries to needy students. He led health projects including at least two sub-district hospitals, three health centres, and eight dispensaries, and served as a member and later chairman of the National Fund for the Disabled of Kenya from 1980. Political detractors have raised controversies, particularly from 1989–1992, with allegations tied to the 1990 murder of Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Ouko. Scotland Yard detective John Troon named Biwott as a person of interest in his final report based on statements by Marianne Brinner-Mattern and Dominico Airgahi, directors of BAK Group, which had been awarded a contract to revamp a molasses plant in Kisumu but was terminated due to failure to raise funding and conduct a feasibility study, later awarded to US company F.C. Schaffer under USAID and the then Minister of Industry Dalmas Otieno. Before Ouko’s death, BAK Group claimed $150,000 in damages; after Ouko’s death, the claim rose to $5.975 million. Airgahi was on bail in Milan in 1987 for fraud and extortion, and Brinner-Mattern was a key witness in that case, with the Milanese judge calling her testimony "unreliable" and recommending a "compassionate veil." Ten government officials, including Biwott, were detained in November 1991, but a Kenyan police investigation found no evidence linking Biwott to Ouko’s disappearance or death. In December 2003, Biwott filed a formal complaint against New Scotland Yard, claiming Troon’s investigation was flawed and erroneous, requesting an investigation into Troon and an apology, which was rejected in December 2004 by the Metropolitan Police, citing lack of involvement of UK citizens or suspects and limited resources, and noting the Kenyan Parliamentary Select Committee (PSC) was investigating Ouko’s death. The PSC proceedings were abruptly terminated when Biwott began giving testimony; the committee, led by Gor Sunguh, refused to allow cross-examination of witnesses by Biwott’s lawyers, with six members resigning and four others leaving. New members were appointed, leaving ten members, four of whom did not sign Sunguh’s report. In 2005, Parliament refused to consider Sunguh’s report, which was re-tabled on 8 December 2010 and rejected as “shoddy” and used to “settle political scores.” In 2000, High Court Judge Alnashir Visram awarded Biwott Sh30 million in damages—the largest in a defamation case in Kenya—for linking him to the Ouko murder in a book titled 'Dr Iain West's Casebook' by Chester Stern and others. The court ordered author and pathologist Iain West and journalist Chester Stern to pay KES 15 million in compensatory and KES 15 million in exemplary damages, and bookshops Bookpoint and Bookstop to pay KES 10 million. Several local dailies were also sued; in March 2002, Kalamaka Ltd., publisher of the People Daily, was found guilty of “unmitigated and defenceless character assassination.”

Mr. Nicholas Biwott was awarded a record Sh30 million in damages, the largest settlement in a defamation case in Kenya, after suing British journalist Chester Stern and others for linking him to the Ouko murder in the book 'Dr Iain West's Casebook'. Chester Stern and the book's publishers, Little Brown, stated they would "vigorously defend" the action but ultimately did not defend it, resulting in an uncontested case. Judge Visram ruled that author and pathologist Iain West and journalist Chester Stern, the book’s co-authors, pay KES 15 million in compensatory damages and another KES 15 million in exemplary damages. Bookpoint and Bookstop, popular Nairobi bookshops, also paid Biwott KES 10 million in damages for stocking copies of 'Dr Ian West's Casebook'. Biwott also sued several local dailies for defamatory coverage; in March 2002, Kalamaka Ltd., the publisher of the People Daily, was found guilty of "unmitigated and defenceless character assassination" and awarded Kshs 20 million in damages. Biwott's case is said to have contributed to the development of defamation law in Kenya and was referenced in 2005 in a defamation and libel case filed by former Chief Justice Evans Gicheru, who sued Andrew Morton, author of the biography 'Moi - The Making of an African Statesman', and publisher Michael O Mara Books. On the morning of 11 July 2017, Biwott died of complications from kidney failure at a Nairobi hospital. A memorial service was held at Milimani AIC on 18 July 2017, and a second service was held at the Maria Soti Girls Educational Centre Kaptarakwa in Keiyo, Elgeyo/Marakwet County, with over 20,000 people attending. In his final speech at the funeral, President Uhuru Kenyatta eulogized Biwott as a "true patriot", stating that when the history of Kenya is written, it will include many men and women who quietly but firmly and confidently contributed to Kenya being a sound, stable country with a growing economy, and that Nicholas Biwott is one of those people. Biwott was buried in a wooden casket, contrary to misleading claims circulating on Kenyan social media prior to his burial that he would be buried in a gold coffin.
